task.goal: Make a nonprofit's public FAQ easier to update when policy answers change.
hard_constraints: One editor has two hours weekly and a static website; no new content system.
Do not publish an answer without a named source and review date.
Track stale answers, conflicting pages and reader failures to find a current answer.
task.available_resources: Existing FAQ files and policy memo archive.

DIRECT_FULL.title: One canonical answer per policy question
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make each policy answer live in exactly one existing static FAQ location. Replace repeated answers elsewhere with descriptive links to that location. This changes the maintenance problem: a policy revision requires one substantive edit instead of several synchronized edits.

For every answer, show the named source document, its archive identifier or date, and the date the editor checked the answer against it. A scheduled next-review date can also support maintenance. If the archive does not support an answer, publish only a notice that the answer is awaiting verification, with a contact route; do not infer policy.

Keep a small spreadsheet or text register beside the existing files: question, canonical URL, source, review date, next review, and known pages that repeat or contradict it. Add a visible “Couldn’t find a current answer?” email link using an existing monitored address. Record the reader’s question and starting page, without retaining unnecessary personal details.

Use the weekly two hours for 20 minutes reviewing new memos and reader reports, 70 minutes updating affected canonical answers and removing conflicting copies, and 30 minutes checking overdue entries and links. Begin with the most frequently changing questions; record remaining duplication as an explicit backlog.

This assumes the editor can edit relevant static pages and access a monitored inbox. External copies remain outside direct control. Links may also make readers take an extra step, so descriptive link wording matters.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Pilot five questions with known repetition. Compare updating one changed policy through canonical answers against the current duplicate-edit process, recording time and missed contradictions. Ask three unfamiliar readers to locate the current answer from different starting pages and identify its source and review date. Inspect the register for overdue answers and unresolved conflicts. The mechanism fails its initial check if duplication remains unnoticed or readers cannot reliably reach the canonical answer.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Trace policy changes to affected answers
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Keep the FAQ’s current structure, but maintain a lightweight dependency register connecting policy memos to every public passage they support. The primary mechanism is change propagation: when a memo changes, the register supplies a concrete checklist of affected answers and potentially conflicting pages.

Use a spreadsheet or plain text file with one row per answer or policy-bearing passage: page location, question, named source and specific section, last review date, next review date, and status. Each published answer also displays its named source and last review date. A new or revised memo triggers review of all linked rows. Search the existing website files for distinctive terms and old wording to catch passages missing from the register. Record contradictory pages until corrected; record unsupported answers for removal or replacement with an awaiting-verification notice.

Spend 25 minutes weekly inspecting archive additions, 65 minutes applying the highest-impact changes, and 30 minutes checking overdue rows, unresolved conflicts, and reader reports. Add a plain email feedback link asking what answer the reader sought and where they looked; log unresolved searches in the same register. Those reports trigger dependency and navigation checks.

This uses the existing files and memo archive without changing publishing infrastructure. It assumes archive changes can be identified and sources are sufficiently specific to map to answers. Initial mapping takes time, so inventory a manageable section each week and mark unmapped sections explicitly. The largest uncertainty is whether the register can stay complete within the editor’s time budget.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Map one FAQ section, then select an archived policy revision whose affected passages can be independently inspected. Compare register-guided review with a simple keyword search of the same files. Count affected passages missed and minutes required, without assuming either method is complete. Submit one simulated failed-search report and verify that it enters the register and leads to a concrete check. Reject or simplify this approach if maintaining dependencies consumes more time than it saves or repeatedly misses relevant pages.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Time-limited answers with a weekly renewal queue
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Give every answer a defined period of validity for publication, then use a weekly renewal queue to prevent unsupported answers from remaining indefinitely. The mechanism is a publication gate: an answer stays available as current guidance only while its documented review remains within its assigned interval.

Add a named source, last review date, and next review date to each answer. Use shorter intervals for policies known to change frequently and longer intervals for stable material; choose initial intervals provisionally because the archive may not establish change frequency. Maintain a plain register sorted by next review date, with columns for conflicting pages and reader failures. Every weekly session also checks new policy memos, which can trigger immediate review before an answer’s scheduled date.

Allocate 20 minutes to new memos and reader feedback, 75 minutes to renewing or replacing due answers, and 25 minutes to finding contradictory wording and updating the register. If an answer cannot be verified, replace its substantive guidance with a clear verification-pending notice and an existing contact route. A visible email link collects reports of missing, confusing, or apparently outdated answers. Log these reports even when the answer is technically current.

This requires only edits to static files and a small register. It assumes the editor can sustain weekly publication and that a contact route already exists. Expiration is handled manually, so missed sessions remain a risk. Review intervals cannot guarantee correctness between checks, and withdrawing answers can reduce usefulness; track pending notices as a backlog, not as successful maintenance.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Pilot a small FAQ section for four weekly sessions, using intervals short enough to exercise renewal. Compare it with a similar section maintained by the existing routine. Inspect overdue published answers, editing time, conflicting passages, and questions left without useful guidance. Ask three readers to distinguish current guidance from a pending notice and find the contact route. The approach fails if renewals exceed the available time, overdue answers remain presented as current, or withdrawals create more unresolved reader failures than the workflow can address.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Use source excerpts to reduce policy rewriting
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Replace selected paraphrased FAQ answers with short, exact excerpts from the policy memo archive, preceded by a plain-language question and a brief statement of who and what the excerpt covers. The primary mechanism is reducing translation work: the editor selects and checks authoritative wording instead of repeatedly reconstructing policy explanations. Keep existing static files and navigation; no new publishing system is required.

Every published answer must display the named source memo, its date and section, and the date the editor reviewed it. Include any conditions or exceptions needed to make the excerpt accurate. If the archive does not establish which conflicting memo governs, replace the substantive answer with a verification-pending notice rather than choosing a policy interpretation.

Keep a plain-text work log alongside the FAQ files. Record each answer’s location, source, review date, next check, and unresolved issues under three labels: stale answer, conflicting page, and reader could not find current guidance. Add an email feedback link using an existing monitored address, asking which question the reader sought and where they looked. Search existing site files for wording from superseded excerpts and related terms whenever a policy changes; log conflicting passages until resolved.

Budget the weekly two hours as 20 minutes checking archive changes and feedback, 70 minutes replacing affected excerpts and correcting conflicting pages, and 30 minutes checking stale entries and reader navigation failures. Start with a small section and expand within that allowance.

This assumes the editor can identify authoritative memos, quote them publicly, and access an existing feedback inbox. It works best when memo passages are short and understandable. Dense, confidential, or interdependent policies may make excerpts unsuitable; their readability and completeness remain unproven.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Prototype three excerpt-based answers and compare them with three manually checked paraphrases covering the same policies, all carrying sources and review dates. Use one archived revision to rehearse an update; record editing time, omitted conditions, and remaining contradictory passages. Ask three unfamiliar readers to find an answer and apply it to a scenario involving an exception. Log a simulated failed-search report and an intentionally overdue review. Reject the approach if excerpts save no editing time, obscure policy conditions, or prevent readers from identifying applicable current guidance.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Maintain policy answers as explicit decision tables
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
For policies whose answers depend on eligibility, dates, or exceptions, replace branching FAQ prose with small decision tables in the existing static pages. Each row states a reader’s circumstances, the applicable answer, and any exception. The mechanism is making policy branches explicit: a change to one eligibility condition becomes a bounded row edit, while overlapping or missing cases become easier to inspect. This could reduce the effort of checking prose that scatters conditions across several answers.

Use the existing memo archive to build one table at a time. Every substantive row must display its named source memo and section plus the date the editor reviewed it. Include effective dates where relevant. Publish a row only when its conditions and answer are supported; unresolved cases receive a verification-pending notice without speculative guidance. Use ordinary HTML tables with clear headers and short introductory instructions; no new content system or generator is needed.

Keep a plain-text issue list beside the files with three categories: stale rows, conflicting pages, and readers unable to find current guidance. Record the affected location, discovery date, and next action. When editing a table, search existing files for the changed condition and previous answer, and log contradictions until corrected. Add a feedback email link if an existing monitored address is available; otherwise, reader checks during the weekly session supply failure reports.

Reserve 20 minutes weekly for new memos and reports, 70 for table updates and conflicting pages, and 30 for overdue reviews and one reader-path check. Initial conversion must fit that same allowance, starting with one small policy family.

This assumes policies can be expressed as a manageable set of cases. Interacting conditions can make tables unwieldy, and a complete-looking table can conceal missing cases. Source interpretation and accessibility still require judgment.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Prototype one table for a policy with an exception. Compare it with the existing prose after checking both against the same memos. Rehearse one archived policy change and record editing time and missed affected passages. Ask three readers to find and apply guidance for an ordinary case, an exception, and an unsupported case. Inspect source and review-date coverage, and log any failed lookup. Reject the approach for that policy if it takes longer to maintain without improving case accuracy, or if readers confidently choose incorrect rows.

EXPAND.title: Publish bounded source excerpts to reduce rewriting
EXPAND.proposal:
Use a short, exact excerpt from the governing memo as the substantive answer wherever it directly resolves the question. The mechanism is reducing editorial interpretation: policy changes require selecting and verifying authoritative wording rather than composing a fresh paraphrase that may introduce exceptions or promises.

The editor pilots a few questions whose answers are stated plainly in the archive. Each answer includes the question, the necessary source excerpt, the named source document and section, and the date reviewed. Include definitions or exceptions needed to preserve meaning. Navigation text may explain where to look, but must not add policy claims. Do not publish an excerpt when its authority, applicability or meaning is uncertain; show a verification-pending notice instead. This approach assumes the selected memo text is suitable for public disclosure. Internal or sensitive material is excluded.

Maintain a plain text register listing each answer’s source, review date, next check, unresolved conflicting pages and reader search failures. Each week, reserve 20 minutes for archive changes and reader reports, 70 minutes for checking and replacing excerpts and correcting conflicting passages, and 30 minutes for stale entries and navigation. An email link to an existing monitored address asks which question the reader could not resolve and where they looked. If no monitored channel exists, record failures through brief observed reader checks during the weekly session.

This needs only the existing files, archive and register. Unlike the prior dependency-register route, it changes how policy becomes public language. It can reduce paraphrase errors, but dense legal wording may increase reader effort, and matching a memo to an answer still requires judgment.
EXPAND.experiment: The editor runs a two-session pilot on four questions with clear source passages. Using an archived revision, prepare excerpt-based updates and ordinary paraphrased updates with the same source checklist. Compare total editing and checking time, omitted qualifications and unsupported claims. Have two unfamiliar readers answer practical questions using each version; record unresolved searches and misunderstandings. Stop the excerpt approach for any question that needs substantial explanation to be usable, or if its time savings disappear after repairing comprehension failures. Retain source and review metadata under either approach.

EXPAND.title: Use reader vocabulary to route people to existing answers
EXPAND.proposal:
Create a small static question index organized around readers’ tasks and wording. The mechanism addresses a different failure: a correct, current answer may already exist but remain undiscoverable because the FAQ uses internal policy terms. Add a prominent “Find an answer” section linking ordinary-language questions and common synonyms to precise FAQ anchors.

Start with one topic and inspect its existing questions and memo terminology. Create a handful of task labels, such as “My circumstances changed,” only where the files support those routes. Index entries should describe questions rather than summarize policy, avoiding another set of answers to maintain. A reader should reach the substantive answer in one or two links. Every destination answer must display its named source and review date before inclusion. Unsupported destinations receive a verification-pending notice instead of guidance.

Keep a small register recording destinations, their next review dates, conflicting pages and failures to find an answer. Add a visible feedback link to an existing monitored inbox, asking what the reader searched for and their starting page. Use reported wording to adjust index labels. Where an answer does not exist, record a content gap rather than repeatedly changing navigation. If no inbox is available, use short observed reader checks to collect failures.

The editor spends 25 minutes weekly checking archive changes and stale answers, 60 minutes updating affected answers and conflicts, and 35 minutes addressing retrieval failures. Limit the index initially to one section so maintenance fits this budget.

This requires static HTML links and a text register. Compared with the prior canonical-answer route, it changes the path into answers rather than their storage. It assumes navigation is a meaningful cause of failure; it cannot resolve ambiguous policy or insufficient source evidence.
EXPAND.experiment: The editor pilots six index links over two weekly sessions. Ask three unfamiliar readers to locate answers to realistic questions using the existing FAQ and the proposed index, alternating task assignments. Record successful arrival at the current answer, time, wrong destinations and editing effort. Include one question with no supported answer to check that navigation does not falsely imply coverage. Stop expanding the index if it produces no additional successful finds, creates misleading routes, or consumes time needed to correct stale guidance. Compare against simply improving the existing FAQ’s link labels.

EXPAND.title: Release policy revisions as complete, checked change sets
EXPAND.proposal:
Treat each policy revision as a small publication transaction. Prepare all necessary edits together and release them only after checking the affected public pages as a group. The mechanism prevents a maintenance session from leaving a mixture of old and new guidance when the editor is interrupted or a revision crosses several pages.

For one revision, create a plain text change sheet containing the named governing memo, effective date if stated, affected FAQ locations, conflicting passages, and completion checks. Find locations through a search of the existing files for policy terms and old wording. The sheet must record uncertainty about coverage; a search is not proof that every affected page was found. Prepare edits in a local copy. Every revised answer must include its named source and review date. Inspect linked pages and qualifications before publishing the group.

Use an existing whole-site upload or versioned deployment if available. If the website only supports individual file replacement, first replace affected substantive answers with source-attributed, dated verification-pending notices, then publish the checked answers. That fallback trades temporary loss of guidance for a visible transition. Keep copies of replaced files, but restore an old substantive answer only if its policy remains valid; otherwise retain the pending notice.

Within each two-hour session, allocate 20 minutes to archive changes, overdue answers and reader reports, 25 to identifying the change set, 55 to preparation, and 20 to release checks. Carry unfinished work forward explicitly. A simple register tracks stale answers, unresolved contradictions and reader failures collected through an existing inbox or brief observed checks.

Unlike the prior dependency-register route, this controls when edits become public. It assumes the editor controls the relevant files; external copies remain unresolved entries. Its main costs are preparation overhead and potentially longer periods with pending notices.
EXPAND.experiment: The editor rehearses one archived revision affecting three pages in a local copy, comparing grouped release with ordinary page-by-page editing. Interrupt each workflow halfway through and inspect what would be public. Measure inconsistent guidance, total work and time without useful answers. Then pilot one small live revision only if the rehearsal fits two hours. Stop using grouped release for that class of change if it provides no reduction in mixed guidance after accounting for additional preparation or pending-notice time. Keep the simpler workflow for isolated edits.

EXPAND.title: Canonical answers with an explicit source-conflict gate
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade the prior “One canonical answer per policy question” route. Keep one substantive answer per question in the existing static files, replace repeated answers with descriptive links, and maintain a text register of canonical URLs, named sources, review dates, next checks, conflicting pages and reader failures.

The consequential change is how the editor handles competing source memos. Before updating a canonical answer, check whether the proposed source explicitly supersedes the old source or clearly applies to different circumstances. A later date alone does not establish authority. Record the relevant passage supporting that decision. If the archive does not resolve the conflict, replace the affected guidance with a dated verification-pending notice naming the competing documents. Keep unaffected, supported answers available. Resume substantive publication only when existing source material resolves the conflict; do not assume the editor can decide policy.

This prevents centralization from spreading one uncertain interpretation across every incoming link. It adds source comparison work and can leave readers without guidance while uncertainty persists. It assumes the editor can edit relevant pages and that the archive sometimes establishes applicability or supersession. Where that prerequisite fails, the pending notice is the fallback, not a guessed answer.

Use the weekly two hours for 20 minutes checking memo changes and reader reports, 70 minutes reviewing sources and updating answers and duplicate pages, and 30 minutes checking stale entries, links and unresolved conflicts. Start with five questions. Collect failed searches through an existing monitored email address, or short observed reader checks if none exists. Preserve replaced files for recovery, but restore old guidance only when its source remains applicable. Mark an interrupted source comparison unresolved so the next session does not mistake a draft for approved guidance.
EXPAND.experiment: The editor pilots five canonical questions over two weekly sessions. In a local copy, use available archived material to examine a clear supersession and an ambiguous source relationship; if the archive lacks either case, label a constructed case as a rehearsal. Compare the upgraded procedure with canonical editing based on a single selected memo. Record editing time, unsupported source choices, stale answers, remaining contradictory pages and time spent without useful guidance. Ask two unfamiliar readers to locate the current answer or recognize that verification is pending, and log failures. Interrupt one comparison and inspect whether its unresolved status survives. Stop expanding if source checks push maintenance beyond two hours or ambiguity still becomes published guidance; retain supported canonical answers and leave unresolved questions visibly pending.

EXPAND.title: Reduce the policy claims the FAQ must maintain
EXPAND.proposal:
Use deliberate retirement and narrowing to reduce the maintenance workload. Unlike centralizing answers or quoting sources, this route changes how much policy the FAQ promises to explain. Test the assumption that every historical FAQ question and every explanatory detail still needs a public answer.

The editor inventories one small section using the existing files and memo archive. Retain practical questions supported by current sources. Remove a question only when the archive explicitly establishes that its program or circumstances no longer apply. Narrow an answer when optional historical detail or additional policy claims can be removed without losing conditions, exceptions or steps needed for the reader's decision. Lack of reader reports is not evidence that an answer is unnecessary. Where continued relevance is uncertain, retain the supported answer and flag it for review.

For retired questions, preserve their existing anchors with a brief, source-attributed and review-dated notice explaining the retirement and linking to a supported successor answer when one exists. Remove obsolete substantive guidance from other controlled pages. Every remaining substantive answer displays its named source and review date. Keep a text register of retained and retired questions, review deadlines, stale answers, conflicting pages and failures to find a current answer.

Allocate 25 minutes weekly to memos and reader reports, 65 minutes to supported updates and selective retirement, and 30 minutes to stale entries, conflicting pages and navigation. Use an existing monitored inbox or brief observed reader checks to capture failures. A report showing that a retired question still represents a current need triggers source review and possible reinstatement. Preserve the former files, but republish their wording only after checking current sources.

This requires no new system. Compared with maintaining every historical answer, fewer claims could mean fewer future edits, at the cost of reduced coverage and possible retrieval failures. Savings are uncertain and depend on finding genuinely obsolete or unnecessary material; if none exists, keep the section intact.
EXPAND.experiment: Within one two-hour session, the editor reviews at most six questions and prepares a local reduced version. Record the number of policy claims and source relationships requiring future maintenance, preparation time, stale guidance and unresolved conflicting pages. Ask two unfamiliar readers to complete practical tasks using the original and reduced versions, including a task reached through a retired question's old anchor. Record whether they find a supported current answer and any missing conditions or unsuccessful searches. Restore material if narrowing removes information needed for a correct decision. Do not publish a retirement without explicit source support. Stop expanding if reader failures increase or the review effort appears greater than the maintenance work removed; retain useful wording and navigation improvements that pass the checks.
